blocks.html: Lesson 4 of 6. Once the vision and goals are set, a steady rhythm of meetings keeps everything moving: weekly team meetings, quarterly planning sessions, and an annual retreat.

blocks.title: Ninety: How to have productive meetings
blocks.note: From ninety.io. A short overview of the meeting discipline your clients will use.

blocks.html:
The Weekly Team Meeting

The heartbeat of the system, run straight from ninety.io's Meetings tool. You'll run the first one or two, then hand it to the team.

  1. Segue: each person shares a bit of personal and professional good news.
  2. Data: a quick scorecard review. Off-track numbers go to the Issues list; no analysis here.
  3. Rocks: a fly-by: on track or off track? Off-track Rocks go to Issues, no discussion.
  4. Headlines: news that matters to the team; use Cascading Messages for other teams.
  5. To-Dos: a five-minute check. Off-track items become Issues.
  6. Issues: the main event. Cull the list, prioritize 5 to 1, and resolve each one: make it a To-Do, move it to Long-Term Issues, or solve it now.
  7. Conclude: recap decisions and rate the meeting 1 to 10. Anyone rating under 9 explains why.

Rotate who runs the agenda so everyone learns the platform, and have a scribe capture To-Dos and decisions.

blocks.html:
Quarterly planning at a glance

  • Objectives, ground rules, check-in, including each person's expectations for the day.
  • Quarter review: Rocks and measurables. After the first annual, add the One-Thing review and a team health check using Lencioni's five dysfunctions. Each leader quietly rates the team 1 to 10 on trust, conflict, commitment, accountability and results; discuss anything below 7 or 8. Low scores usually trace back to trust.
  • 9 core competencies and org fitness: is the org chart strong, are seats well defined, does every seat have KPIs, and are the right people in them?
  • Focus Filters check, then operating system upgrades and any key topics.
  • Set 3 to 7 SMART Rocks for the next 90 days, then core function and individual Rocks.
  • Long-Term Issues with Raise, Discuss, Resolve.
  • Next steps: confirm To-Dos and the date of the next quarterly or annual. Then rate the meeting.

A 90% hit rate on Rocks, To-Dos and measurables counts as a 10.

blocks.prompt: During the Data section of a Weekly Team Meeting, a KPI is way off target. What happens?
options: The team stops to analyze it right away
It goes on the Issues list to be discussed later in the meeting
The owner explains it to the CEO privately
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Identify it, drop it to Issues, keep moving.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Off-track numbers go to the Issues list. Discussion happens during the Issues section, not during data review.

blocks.prompt: A team member rates the weekly meeting a 7. What should happen?
options: They briefly explain why and suggest how it could be better
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. Anyone under 9 explains, so the meeting keeps improving.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Anyone rating below 9 briefly explains why and suggests an improvement.

blocks.prompt: What are the three ways to resolve an issue in the Weekly Team Meeting?
options: Ignore it, delay it, or delegate it
Make it a To-Do, move it to Long-Term Issues, or solve it now
Email, call, or schedule a meeting
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Make it a To-Do, move it to the Long-Term Issues list for the quarterly or annual, or solve it on the spot.

blocks.prompt: In the quarterly team health check, what do low scores usually trace back to?
blocks.feedbackCorrect: Right. Trust is the foundation of Lencioni's model.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Low team health scores usually trace back to trust.

blocks.prompt: How long is the annual planning retreat?
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: The annual retreat is a two-day off-site session.

blocks.promptHtml:
You're observing a client's third Weekly Team Meeting, which they now run themselves. It started 10 minutes late, the team spent 35 minutes debating why the sales number was down during the Data section, never reached the Issues list, and ended without creating a single To-Do. Ratings were all 8s and 9s.

Afterwards, the integrator asks for your feedback. Write what you'd tell her.
rubric: Starts with something genuinely positive and keeps the tone coaching, not critical
Points out that off-track data should go to the Issues list instead of being debated during the Data section
Explains that the Issues section is the main event, and that resolving issues means creating To-Dos with owners
Addresses discipline: same day and time, starting and ending on time, and honest ratings with explanations below 9
Leaves her with one or two specific changes for next week rather than taking over the meeting
blocks.coachContext: This is OneAccord's 'Mastering OASYS: Becoming a Certified Implementer' course for principals who will coach clients through OASYS. OASYS is OneAccord's Business Operating System (BOS), built on the Ninety OS model and run on ninety.io; older materials say 'SPE' (Strategic Planning and Execution) and Doug says 'Oasis'. Doug Hall presents the videos and helped launch the practice but is no longer the practice lead; OneAccord has no current practice lead and Nick Anderson is the contact. The implementer is a BOS COACH: teaches the system and ninety.io, models and facilitates meetings, monitors ninety.io usage, holds the leadership team accountable, sets quarterly planning dates on a rolling 12-month basis and the next annual retreat date, builds trust, helps the team discover its own answers (Raise, Discuss, Resolve), and does NOT run day-to-day operations. Market: the 'BOS upgrade market' - companies of roughly 20 to 500 employees that already have a BOS (their current way of leading and managing, a level above functions like sales, ops, finance); the work is with the leadership team (owner/CEO plus the 3-7 direct reports who manage functions; about 5 is ideal). All BOS frameworks (EOS, Scaling Up, 4DX, OKRs, Great Game of Business) share the same underlying ideas from Gerber, Harnish, Lencioni, Collins and others; OASYS adopts Ninety's vocabulary co-branded as OneAccord OASYS. Owner objectives: achieve purpose and goals; increase time freedom via a self-managing company; optimize enterprise value (reduce owner dependence, improve financial performance). Six upgrade strategies: equip the leadership team with tools and methods; right people and culture; alignment on a vision; right goals and objectives; right KPIs; execution accountability. The 'secret sauce' is connecting strategy to execution. Ten success indicators (reviewed with clients quarterly): solid strategy, shared vision, right people in right seats, great teamwork, right numbers, consistent execution, solving issues, getting the right stuff done (90-day cadence), financial performance, enterprise value. Ninety's 9 core competencies: vision, customer, goals, people, structure (some versions say culture), data, meetings, process, enterprise value. Roadmap: assessments/conversations -> situation analysis and proposal -> owner/CEO agreement -> baseline (ninety.io account, lightweight CSP/business assessment, enterprise value appraisal, behavioral assessments such as DISC/Predictive Index/Culture Index, work-style tools such as Working Genius or Kolbe) -> three implementation workshops (Foundation, Vision, Goal Setting) -> coach weekly meetings ('teach one, coach one'; doing more than two makes the client dependent) -> set quarterly planning dates for a rolling 12 months -> first annual 2-day retreat about a year in -> quarterly cycle until graduation. Kickoff: CSM finalizes the SOW, office sends it via DocuSign and issues the first invoice; coach schedules a 60-90 minute kickoff with key leaders; sets up the client's ninety.io account with Abby following the 'Onboarding a Client to Ninety.io' SOP; sends a welcome packet (OASYS overview, ninety.io intro, roles and expectations, pre-work); kickoff agenda: review BOS-upgrade goals, timeline and milestones, orient to ninety.io, assign a client BOS Champion; lock in all implementation meeting dates and send invites before the call ends. Workshop logistics: senior leaders only; a no-interruption venue, off-site if the office will distract; about 7 hours (+/- 1), oriented to objectives not filling time; in person is best, virtual works with breaks about every hour; ideally 2-4 weeks apart so behaviors sink in, so the three workshops form the client's first quarter. The coach chooses methods; outcomes matter. The order of foundational meetings can flex to client needs (e.g. urgent people issues, existing clear vision), but all elements eventually get covered. Facilitation: published agenda, timekeeping, active listening, respectful dialogue, guide don't dominate, open-ended questions, draw out quiet voices, summarize, drive to decisions, assign who/what/when in ninety.io, confirm next steps. Foundation Setting: objectives and ground rules (finish time, breaks together, no devices, kind but honest, advance the conversation, confidentiality); check-in and shift to working ON the business; set expectation of an 18-24 month journey; Org Fitness baseline; 5 Stages of Development / 'hitting the ceiling'; org chart (structure first, people second; look 6-12 months out; one accountable person per core function; seats with Roles/Accountabilities/Responsibilities; Visionary and 2iC; fill seats using CCC: Competency, Commitment, Capacity; aim for 80% right); Rocks (3-7 SMART company 90-day priorities, long-term issues prioritized 5 to 1); Scorecard (about 15 KPIs, ~3 per core function, each with an owner and target, reviewed weekly, missed targets go to Issues, 13 weeks at a glance); Meetings discipline (same day, time, agenda, start and end on time; Raise, Discuss, Resolve; decide who runs meetings and who updates ninety.io); homework; conclude with feedback and a 1-10 rating. Vision Setting: turn expectations into agreements; Focus Filters: core values (3-7, discovered not created, used to hire/fire/review/reward/recognize, fit check), industry and niche, compelling why (not about money, bigger than a goal), ideal customer (geographics, demographics, psychographics), compelling value proposition (innovation, cost, service, status); Compelling and Audacious Goal (at least 5 years out, bold, SMART, consistent with focus filters); homework: finalize values, core values speech at an all-hands, enter focus filters in ninety.io Vision. Goal Setting: 3-year goals (date, 1-3 financial goals, 1-3 KPIs, envision, agree transparency level); 1-year goals (3-7 goals or no more than the number of senior leaders, numerical and operational); set Rocks; tackle issues with RDR. OneAccord's own decks combine Vision and Goal Setting into one workshop, and there is an optional Sales Engine workshop. Weekly Team Meeting (run in ninety.io): Segue (personal and professional good news), Data/Scorecard (identify off-track numbers, add to Issues, no deep analysis), Rocks fly-by (on/off track; off-track to Issues), Headlines (cascading messages for other teams), To-Dos (5-minute check; off-track to Issues), Issues (cull, prioritize 5-1, resolve by To-Do, move to long-term, or solve), Conclude (recap and rate 1-10; anyone rating under 9 explains why). A scribe captures To-Dos and decisions. Quarterly planning: objectives and ground rules, check-in and expectations, quarter review (rocks, measurables, One-Thing promises, team health using Lencioni's five dysfunctions: trust, conflict, commitment, accountability, results, each rated 1-10; about 90% hit rate counts as a 10), 9 core competencies and org fitness review, focus filters check, operating system upgrades, key topics, set 3-7 SMART rocks, long-term issues via RDR, next steps (confirm next QPM/APM), conclude and rate. Ideally in person, every 90 days. Annual planning retreat: two days off-site. Day 1: progress reviews, team health, 9 core competencies, SWOT, vision and focus filters, 3-year goals. Day 2: 3-year recap, key topics, 1-year goals, rocks, long-term issues, next steps. Graduation = client moves into self-management of its BOS. It can be the coach's or the client's decision, timely or premature. Premature graduation is when the client is not about 80% strong across the 9 core competencies; common causes: budget crunch, chemistry mismatch with the coach, unresolved leadership-team dysfunction (e.g. a COO wanting to prove they can run it). Risks of self-management: quarterly rigor backslides, schedules stretch, self-facilitated sessions go poorly (you can't read the label from inside the jar), the CEO loses an advisor and the leadership team loses a coach. Respond by protecting a third-party facilitator for quarterlies/annuals, offering a lighter or lower-cost option, or helping them find another facilitator or peer group. Competitors: EOS/Traction sets the mark; Doug calls EOS the 'Toyota Camry' of operating systems, a reliable 80% solution, but rigid ('EOS pure', like a franchise that can't change the menu). OASYS is equally granular, built on Ninety's 9 core competencies versus EOS's 6 components, adds depth in strategy, financial literacy and culture, and is flexible (can change the order of sessions and add best-in-class tools) while still structured. Don't trash competitors. ninety.io: get access via Abby; learn through Knowledge > 'The 90 Way' and ninety.io resources; practice in a free trial company, not in OneAccord's real account. Ninety.io templates must be rebranded to OneAccord standards before client use.
